delta.text: **Theorem (Klein).** Any 5 points in the plane, no three collinear, contain 4 that are the vertices of a convex qu

adrilateral.

## Two facts used

**Fact 1 (hull vertices are extreme).** Let S be a finite point set and A a vertex of the convex hull of S. Then A is not in the convex hull of S

∖{A}. In particular A lies in no triangle formed by three other points of S.
Reason: a polygon vertex is an extreme point, and an extreme point cannot be a nontrivial convex combination of other points of the set.

**Fact 2 (conv

ex-position test).** Four points in general position form a convex quadrilateral iff none of them lies in the triangle formed by the other three.
Reason: their convex hull is a polygon with 3 or 4 vertices, all

from the set. If it has 3 vertices, the fourth point lies in that triangle, and strictly inside since no three are collinear. If it has 4, the points are the vertices of a convex quadrilateral.

## Proof

Let the
points be in general position and let H be their convex hull. H is a convex polygon whose vertices are among the 5 points. It has at least 3 vertices, since no three points

are collinear. Split on the number of hull vertices.

**Case 5 vertices.** Take any 4 of the points. Each is a hull vertex, so by Fact 1 none lies in the triangle of the

other three. By Fact 2 they form a convex quadrilateral.

**Case 4 vertices.** The 4 hull vertices form a convex quadrilateral by definition.

**Case 3 vertices.** Call the hull triangle ABC and

the remaining points D, E. D and E lie strictly inside ABC, because a point on an edge would be collinear with two vertices.

Let ℓ be the line through D and E. ℓ passes

through none of A, B, C, since that would give three collinear points. So each of A, B, C lies strictly on one side of ℓ.

They cannot all lie on the same

side: the triangle is the convex hull of A, B, C, so it would sit entirely in that open half-plane, yet D is on ℓ and inside the triangle. Hence two vertices lie on one side and one on the other. Relabel so A and

B lie on the same side, call it the open half-plane H⁺, and C on the other.

**Claim: A, B, D, E form a convex quadrilateral.** By Fact 2, check that none is in

the triangle of the other three.

- **A is not in triangle BDE.** A is a hull vertex of all 5 points, so Fact 1 applies. Same for B and triangle ADE.
- **D is not in triangle ABE.** Any
point of triangle ABE is λA + μB + νE with nonnegative weights summing to 1. Its signed distance to ℓ is λ·d(A) + μ·d(B), where d(A), d(B) > 0. This is zero only when

λ = μ = 0, i.e. the point is E itself. D lies on ℓ and D ≠ E, so D is not in triangle ABE.
- **E is not in triangle ABD.** Identical argument with D and E swapped.

So

no one of A, B, D, E lies in the triangle of the other three, and by Fact 2 they are the vertices of a convex quadrilateral.

All cases yield a convex quadrilateral. ∎

## Why general position is needed

Drop it and the
statement fails: take three collinear points plus two more anywhere. Every 4-subset then contains three collinear points, or a point on
a segment between two others, so no 4 form a strictly convex quadrilateral. The proof uses the hypothesis in exactly three places: the hull has at least 3 vertices,
D and E are strictly interior, and ℓ avoids A, B, C.
